Sufficiently
suf-fi'shent-ly
adv. (to a sufficient degree; enough; adequately)
From sufficient, Latin sufficere, to be enough, from sub- and facere, to make under or supply. The idea is supply that meets the need exactly — neither short nor superfluous.

Biblical Definition

The adverb appears twice, and the two uses face opposite directions. The first is an honest confession of shortfall in Hezekiah's passover: “For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, neither had the people gathered themselves together to Jerusalem” (2Ch 30:3). The feast had to be moved a month because the ministers were not ready — a remarkable admission for Scripture to record about the clergy, and a standing rebuke to any notion that the ordinances may be handled carelessly. The second is a promise of enough: Tyre's merchandise shall at last be holiness to the LORD, “for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” (Isa 23:18). The servants of God are promised food enough and clothing that lasts — not abundance for hoarding, since the same verse says it shall not be treasured nor laid up. Behind both stands the great New Testament use of the root, which places all sufficiency outside the man: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2Co 3:5); and the Lord's own word to Paul, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sufficiently as to a sufficient degree; enough; to a degree that answers the purpose or gives content.

expand to see more

SUFFI'CIENTLY, adv.

To a sufficient degree; enough; to a degree that answers the purpose, or gives content; as, we are sufficiently supplied with food.

A man sufficiently qualified for the office.

The Latin sufficere is to be enough, to suffice; the idea is a supply adequate to the need.

The priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently. 2 Chron. 30.

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 30:3 — "For they could not keep it at that time, because the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently, neither had the people gathered themselves together to Jerusalem."

Isaiah 23:18 — "And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing."

2 Corinthians 3:5 — "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;"

2 Corinthians 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Modern Corruption

Self-sufficiency is preached as a virtue and enough is treated as a failure, so the one thing Scripture calls sufficient is the one thing men will not accept.

expand to see more

The culture's highest compliment is self-sufficiency, and 2 Corinthians 3:5 denies a man even the capacity to think anything as of himself. That is a total claim, and it is the death of the self-made ministry as much as of the self-made man. The corruption enters the church whenever competence is treated as the qualification and the sufficiency is located in gifting, training, or platform. Paul was the ablest man in the first century and disclaimed sufficiency for a thought.

The other corruption is dissatisfaction with enough. Isaiah 23:18 promises food sufficient and clothing durable, and explicitly rules out treasuring and laying up — which most readers experience as a disappointment rather than a promise. And 2 Corinthians 12:9 is routinely quoted as a consolation prize for people whose prayers were declined, when it is in fact the answer: the grace is the sufficiency, and the weakness is where the strength is perfected. A church that cannot preach enough as a blessing will always be vulnerable to a gospel of more.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lemadai, to sufficiency; Greek hikanos (G2425), sufficient, competent; arkeo (G714), to be enough; Latin sufficere.

expand to see more

Hebrew lemikhsah and lesobe'ah — for covering and for satisfying; Isaiah 23:18, food to the full and clothing that lasts.

Greek hikanoi (G2425) — sufficient, competent, adequate; 2 Corinthians 3:5, denied to the self and granted from God.

Greek hikanotes (G2426) — sufficiency; the noun in the same verse, our sufficiency is of God.

Greek arkei (G714) — it is enough, it suffices; 2 Corinthians 12:9, my grace is sufficient for thee.

Latin sufficere, from sub- and facere — to supply underneath; Webster's root, a supply that meets the need.

Usage

"“The priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently” — the feast waited a month for unready ministers."

"“To eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” — enough, and not laid up."

"“Our sufficiency is of God” — not even a thought is self-supplied."
